The age at which these fish complete the transition from an endotrophic to an exotrophic existence is well defined; following fertilization, the yolk-sac larva emerges and completes absorption of its endogenous reserves over a period of three days [ab = three days] at the same ambient temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This brief lecithotrophic phase, calculated from the sum of hatching and yolk-sac absorption durations, is consistent with the rapid developmental rates observed in tropical reef fishes that face high predation pressure during the early larval stages. The exact timing of the point of no return is critical for larval survival in the pelagic environment.

Females of Lutjanus gibbus attain puberty at a relatively modest body size, with sexual maturation occurring when the fork length reaches 21.5 centimeters [Lp = 21.5 centimeters]. This length-based threshold corresponds to an estimated wet weight at puberty of approximately 140 grams [Wwp = approximately 140 grams], a derivation based on the length-weight relationship parameterized for this species. The relationship between length and mass is strongly allometric, and this pubertal mass represents a significant fraction of the ultimate weight the fish will achieve. Reaching this developmental milestone allows the female to participate in the seasonal spawning aggregations that are characteristic of many reef-dwelling serranids and lutjanids, though the onset of gametogenesis may be further modulated by local environmental cues such as photoperiod and water temperature. The relatively early attainment of sexual maturity is an important life-history trait that influences population resilience to fishing pressure across the Indo-Pacific range of this species.

The maximum size attainable by the humpback red snapper has been documented through field surveys, which indicate an ultimate fork length of 56.8 centimeters [Li = 56.8 centimeters]. A fish of this length would have an associated ultimate wet weight of 2515 grams [Wwi = 2515 grams], as estimated from the species-specific length-mass conversion. This asymptotic dimension suggests a moderately large-bodied predator within the Lutjanidae family. The growth trajectory from the earliest post-settlement juvenile stage to this terminal size is relatively protracted, with individuals investing heavily in somatic growth before shifting resources toward reproduction. Comparisons with congeneric species reveal that Lutjanus gibbus occupies an intermediate position in terms of maximal body size, being smaller than the cubera snapper but larger than the blacktail snapper. The ecological implications of attaining a 56.8-centimeter fork length include access to a wider range of piscine prey and reduced vulnerability to gape-limited predators.

Egg diameter data from the closely related species Lutjanus stellatus provide a basis for estimating the initial mass of a newly fertilized ovum in Lutjanus gibbus. Assuming a spherical egg of 0.9 millimeters in diameter, the calculated wet weight at birth is 0.00038 grams [Wwb = 0.00038 grams]. This extraordinarily small initial mass, typical of pelagic-spawning teleosts that produce buoyant eggs, means that the newly emerged yolk-sac larva must begin exogenous feeding within days to avoid starvation. The tiny size at hatching contrasts sharply with the eventual 2515-gram ultimate wet weight of the adult, representing a mass increase of over six orders of magnitude across the lifespan. Resources directed toward vitellogenesis must therefore generate a very large number of these minute oocytes to ensure that at least some offspring survive the high mortality rates of the planktonic larval phase. The energetic cost of producing such small propagules is amortized over a potentially long reproductive lifespan.

The maximum lifespan of Lutjanus gibbus in its natural environment has been estimated from tag-return and otolith increment data, with the oldest documented individuals reaching 18 years [am = 18 years] under the thermal regimes typical of tropical coral reef habitats at 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This longevity, while considerable, is not extreme among the Lutjanidae; several congeneric species are known to persist for three decades or more. The life-history trade-off between early maturation and extended senescence appears to be mediated by the relatively stable food availability and low abiotic stress in the species' preferred reef environments. Somatic senescence in older individuals is likely accompanied by a gradual decline in reproductive output, though fecundity may remain high well into the second decade of life. Understanding the natural mortality schedule and age structure of populations is critical for developing sustainable harvest strategies, as the species supports important commercial and artisanal fisheries throughout its distribution from the Red Sea to the central Pacific Ocean.
